--- title: "Lesson 12 · Causal inference: from association to effect" subtitle: "Part III · Causal inference, measurement and disease burden" description: "Potential outcomes, identification assumptions, g-computation, propensity scores and inverse probability weighting, positivity, and sensitivity to unmeasured confounding." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3.5 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 8–9]{} [Threads: bias · uncertainty · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} [ ]{.pm-label} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - state a causal question as a contrast between potential outcomes, under a well-defined intervention; - explain exchangeability, positivity and consistency, and why each is needed; - estimate a marginal causal effect by g-computation, and explain why it can differ from an adjusted odds ratio; - estimate the same effect by inverse probability weighting, check balance and diagnose positivity problems; - quantify how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain away an estimate. ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** Policy questions are causal: how many cases of childhood asthma would a 10 µg/m³ reduction in NO₂ prevent? An adjusted odds ratio from Lesson 9 doesn't answer that directly. Causal inference makes the question precise, says which assumptions the answer depends on, and provides estimators that target the answer itself. ::: ## 12.1 Potential outcomes: two worlds, one observed {#s1} Imagine two worlds. In one, every child lives with the NO₂ they actually had. In the other, an intervention has reduced every child's NO₂ by Δ µg/m³. Each child has a **potential outcome** in each world. The **causal effect** compares the two worlds for the same children. Real data show only the first world. Here, because the data are simulated, both can be shown. ```{=html}
asthma in both worldsasthma prevented by the reductionno asthma in either world
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$Y_i^{x}: \text{ outcome of child } i \text{ if exposure were set to } x$$ $$RR_{\text{causal}} = \frac{E[Y^{X-\Delta}]}{E[Y^{X}]}, \qquad RD_{\text{causal}} = E[Y^{X-\Delta}] - E[Y^{X}]$$ ::: {.note} Only $Y_i^{X_i}$, the outcome under the exposure actually received, is ever observed (consistency). ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r # the causal question, written as a contrast: # E[asthma | everyone's NO2 lowered by 10] # vs E[asthma | NO2 as observed] # Identification needs: # exchangeability given (SES, green) # positivity: every child could have had # NO2 10 µg/m3 lower # consistency: "lowering NO2" is well defined ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $Y_i^{x}$: child $i$'s potential outcome: whether they would have asthma if their exposure were set to $x$. - $E[Y^{X}]$: the average outcome if everyone kept their actual exposure. - $E[Y^{X-\Delta}]$: the average outcome if everyone's exposure were lowered by $\Delta$ (here 10 µg/m³): a hypothetical intervention. - $RR_{\text{causal}}$: the causal risk ratio: average risk under the intervention divided by average risk without it. - $RD_{\text{causal}}$: the causal risk difference: cases prevented per child; × 1,000 for cases per 1,000. :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#poReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @hernan2020causal develop causal inference from potential outcomes; @hernan2016using on framing observational analyses as emulations of a target trial; @greenland1999confounding on the formal definition of confounding. ::: ## 12.2 G-computation: estimating the two worlds from data {#s2} **G-computation**, also called standardization, estimates each world with an outcome model. Fit a regression of asthma on NO₂ and confounders; predict every child's risk with their own NO₂, and again with NO₂ lowered by Δ; average each set of predictions; compare. The result is a **marginal** effect for this population, the quantity the policy question asks for, and it can be compared directly with the truth from 12.1. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\widehat{E}[Y^{x}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{P}(Y = 1 \mid X = x_i,\ Z = z_i)$$ ::: {.note} Evaluated once with each child's own $x_i$, once with $x_i - \Delta$; $Z$ = confounders. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green, family = binomial, data = cohort) r1 <- mean(predict(fit, cohort, type = "response")) r0 <- mean(predict(fit, mutate(cohort, no2_true = no2_true - 10), type = "response")) c(rr = r0 / r1, rd = r0 - r1) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\widehat{E}[Y^{x}]$: the estimated average outcome if exposure were set to $x$ for everyone. - $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}$: average over all children: g-computation predicts each child's risk, then averages. - $\widehat{P}$: the predicted risk from the fitted outcome model (here logistic regression). - $x_i$: child $i$'s exposure, set to the value of the scenario (actual, or 10 µg/m³ lower). - $z_i$: child $i$'s confounders, kept at their observed values. :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#gcReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): g-computation with a bootstrap confidence interval"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gcomp <- function(d, delta = 10) { fit <- glm(asthma ~ no2_true + ses + green, family = binomial, data = d) r_obs <- mean(predict(fit, d, type = "response")) r_int <- mean(predict(fit, mutate(d, no2_true = no2_true - delta), type = "response")) c(rr = r_int / r_obs, cases_prevented_per_1000 = 1000 * (r_obs - r_int)) } gcomp(cohort) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> rr cases_prevented_per_1000 #> 0.8880198 15.3636874 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(12) boot <- map(1:200, \(b) as_tibble_row(gcomp(slice_sample(cohort, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))) |> bind_rows() apply(boot, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> rr cases_prevented_per_1000 #> 2.5% 0.7689192 0.4975408 #> 97.5% 0.9963491 31.5739105 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} Reading an adjusted odds ratio as a population effect. The aOR is conditional on the covariates, and because odds ratios are non-collapsible it differs from the marginal OR even without confounding. G-computation turns a model into the marginal risk ratio or risk difference the question asks for. ::: **Two ways.** Two routes to the uncertainty of the same causal estimate: resampling the data (bootstrap) or drawing from the posterior. ```{=html}
Two ways · G-computation
Frequentist
Bayesian
``` ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @snowden2011implementation demonstrate g-computation step by step; @hernan2020causal treat standardization and the g-formula; @keiding2014standardization link it to classical standardization. ::: ## 12.3 Propensity scores and inverse probability weighting {#s3} A second route models the **exposure** instead of the outcome. The **propensity score** is each child's probability of high NO₂ (here ≥ 30 µg/m³) given the confounders. Weighting each child by the inverse probability of the exposure they actually had creates a pseudo-population in which the confounders are balanced between exposed and unexposed. Check the overlap and the balance, and see what happens if the propensity model includes a variable that predicts exposure strongly but isn't a confounder. ```{=html}

Propensity model for high NO₂ (≥ 30 µg/m³):

high NO₂lower NO₂
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$e(z) = P(A = 1 \mid Z = z), \qquad w_i = \frac{A_i}{e(z_i)} + \frac{1 - A_i}{1 - e(z_i)}$$ $$\widehat{E}[Y^{a}] = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, 1\{A_i = a\}\, Y_i}{\sum_i w_i\, 1\{A_i = a\}}$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r d <- cohort |> mutate(high = no2_true >= 30) ps <- glm(high ~ ses + green, family = binomial, data = d) |> fitted() d$w <- ifelse(d$high, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps)) with(d, weighted.mean(asthma[high], w[high]) / weighted.mean(asthma[!high], w[!high])) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $e(z)$: the propensity score: the probability of high exposure given the confounders $z$. - $A_i$: child $i$'s exposure group: 1 if highly exposed, 0 if not. - $w_i$: the inverse probability weight: rarely exposed children with high exposure (and vice versa) count more. - $e(z_i)$: child $i$'s own propensity score. - $\widehat{E}[Y^{a}]$: the weighted average outcome in group $a$: an estimate of the average outcome if everyone had exposure $a$. :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#psReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): weights, balance and the weighted risk ratio"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- cohort |> mutate(high = no2_true >= 30) ps_fit <- glm(high ~ ses + green, family = binomial, data = d) d <- d |> mutate(ps = fitted(ps_fit), w = if_else(high, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps))) smd <- function(x, g, w) { m1 <- weighted.mean(x[g], w[g]); m0 <- weighted.mean(x[!g], w[!g]) (m1 - m0) / sqrt((var(x[g]) + var(x[!g])) / 2) } tibble(variable = c("ses", "green"), before = c(smd(d$ses, d$high, rep(1, nrow(d))), smd(d$green, d$high, rep(1, nrow(d)))), after = c(smd(d$ses, d$high, d$w), smd(d$green, d$high, d$w))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 2 × 3 #> variable before after #> #> 1 ses -0.417 -0.0753 #> 2 green -1.98 -0.329 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} with(d, weighted.mean(asthma[high], w[high]) / weighted.mean(asthma[!high], w[!high])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 1.219046 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(d$w) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 1.000 1.029 1.131 1.892 1.515 93.259 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @austin2011introduction introduces propensity score methods; @cole2008constructing on constructing and checking inverse probability weights; @westreich2010positivity on positivity violations in practice. ::: ## 12.4 How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be? {#s4} Every observational estimate assumes no unmeasured confounding. The **E-value** asks: how strongly would an unmeasured confounder need to be associated with both the exposure and the outcome (as risk ratios) to fully explain away the observed association? Here, pretend green space had not been measured, and see how the estimate and its E-value compare. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$E = RR + \sqrt{RR\,(RR - 1)}$$ $$\text{explains away if } \frac{RR_{EU}\, RR_{UD}}{RR_{EU} + RR_{UD} - 1} \ge RR$$ ::: {.note} $RR_{EU}$: confounder–exposure association; $RR_{UD}$: confounder–outcome association. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r e_value <- function(rr) rr + sqrt(rr * (rr - 1)) e_value(1.12) # point estimate e_value(1.01) # lower confidence limit # or: EValue::evalues.RR(1.12, lo = 1.01) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $E$: the E-value: the minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need, with both exposure and outcome, to explain the RR away. - $RR$: the observed risk ratio (inverted if below 1). - $RR_{EU}$: the confounder–exposure association (as a risk ratio). - $RR_{UD}$: the confounder–outcome association (as a risk ratio). :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#evReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Bayesian preview"} In a Bayesian analysis, g-computation is done on every posterior draw of the outcome model, giving a full posterior for the causal risk ratio. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding can be expressed as a prior on the bias parameters, so that uncertainty about the confounder enters the final interval (probabilistic bias analysis, Lesson 13). ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @vanderweele2017sensitivity introduced the E-value; @fox2021applying on quantitative bias analysis more generally; @hernan2020causal on the role of each identification assumption. ::: ## 12.5 Negative controls: looking for hidden confounding {#s5} The E-value asks how strong unmeasured confounding would *need* to be. A **negative control** looks for evidence that it is actually there. A **negative control outcome** is an outcome the exposure cannot plausibly cause, but which shares the main outcome's confounders. If the exposure appears to affect it, the same bias is probably at work in the main analysis. Here the negative control outcome is dental caries: NO₂ doesn't cause tooth decay, but caries, like asthma, is more common in deprived households, with parental smoking and with less green space. ```{=html}
``` A good negative control shares the main analysis's sources of bias, and is unaffected by the exposure. Its mirror image is a **negative control exposure**: an exposure that cannot affect the outcome but shares the main exposure's confounders, such as pollution measured *after* the outcome occurred (Lesson 15 uses tomorrow's pollution). Negative controls detect bias; on their own they don't correct it, although extensions use them to adjust estimates. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): a negative control outcome"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(12) nc <- cohort |> mutate(caries = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.3 - 0.5 * ses + 0.4 * parent_smoke - 0.5 * (green - 0.5))), x = no2_true / 10) broom::tidy(glm(caries ~ x + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex, family = binomial, data = nc), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "x") # should be close to 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #> term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high #> #> 1 x 1.02 0.0613 0.276 0.783 0.902 1.15 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @lipsitch2010negative introduced negative controls to epidemiology; @shi2020selective review the methods, including bias correction with negative controls. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - A causal effect compares potential outcomes for the same population under two well-defined interventions. Only one is ever observed. - Identifying it from data needs exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding), positivity and consistency. - G-computation predicts both worlds from an outcome model and averages, giving marginal risk ratios and risk differences. - Inverse probability weighting balances confounders by weighting; check balance, overlap and extreme weights. - Don't put non-confounders that strongly predict exposure into a propensity model: they worsen positivity and precision. - E-values express how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain an association away. ## Concepts at a glance {#concepts} Ideas from this lesson that are easily confused, side by side. | Concept | What it is | How it differs | |---|---|---| | **Potential outcomes** | The outcomes a person would have under each exposure level. | Only one is observed: the missing one is the causal inference problem. | | **Average treatment effect** | The difference in mean potential outcomes in the population. | A marginal effect; a regression coefficient is a conditional effect. | | **Marginal vs conditional odds ratio** | Population-averaged vs within strata of covariates. | Differ for odds ratios even without confounding (non-collapsibility). | | **G-computation** | Predict everyone's outcome under each exposure with an outcome model, then average. | Models the outcome; IPW models the exposure. | | **Inverse probability weighting** | Reweight people by the inverse of their probability of the exposure they had. | Models the exposure (propensity score); creates a balanced pseudo-population. | | **Exchangeability vs positivity** | No unmeasured confounding vs everyone having a chance of each exposure level. | Both needed; positivity can be checked in data, exchangeability can't. | | **E-value** | How strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain the estimate away. | A sensitivity measure, not a test or a correction. | | **Negative control** | An outcome the exposure can't cause, or an exposure that can't cause the outcome, sharing the main analysis's biases. | Detects bias rather than correcting it; the E-value instead asks how strong hidden bias would need to be. | | **Negative control outcome vs exposure** | Swap the outcome (e.g., dental caries) vs swap the exposure (e.g., tomorrow's pollution). | Each detects only biases it shares with the main analysis. | ```{=html}
